title: Joint Text-Audio Alignment for EEG-to-Text Decoding in Chinese Speech Production and Perception

images.desc:
3.2 The EEGAlign framework


To overcome the limitations of the CTC-only decoder, we propose EEGAlign. A natural extension would be to introduce sentence-level semantic supervision by aligning EEG representations with pretrained text embeddings. However, EEGAlign is built on the core view that semantic and acoustic supervision are complementary rather than interchangeable.


Sentence-level text semantic alignment provides a stable global target for distinguishing among thousands of Chinese sentences, whereas audio acoustic alignment supplies temporally structured information related to pronunciation, rhythm, and sub-second speech dynamics. Because the two supervision signals target different granularities of language representation, they are complementary rather than interchangeable. Accordingly, EEGAlign augments the CTC decoding path with two auxiliary alignment axes: semantic alignment to frozen BGE-M3 text embeddings and acoustic alignment to wav2vec 2.0 speech features.


Figure 1 provides an overview. Rather than treating the method as a rigid architecture, we organize it around one core requirement: the encoder must support three levels of supervision at once—shared subject-agnostic structure, subject-specific adaptation, and cross-modal alignment at both sentence and chunk levels.


Figure 1: Overall architecture of EEGAlign. A shared sequence encoder with lightweight subject-specific adapters maps EEG to latent representations. A learned upsampler restores temporal density before applying three joint heads: CTC for decoding, text semantic alignment to BGE-M3 text embeddings, and audio acoustic alignment to wav2vec 2.0 features.

4.7 Analysis


This section provides a detailed analysis of the inference-time fusion gain, candidate-set sensitivity, and audio-alignment weight sensitivity. We further examine whether the semantic branch reshapes the encoder representation itself, with complementary paradigm-specific analyses deferred to Appendix G.


Fusion gain over CTC-only ranking. We compare EEGAlign’s default fused score sDAs^{\mathrm{DA}} (Eq. 5, α=0.4\alpha=0.4) to the degenerate case of ranking candidates by the CTC log-likelihood only, using the same trained model. Figure 2(a) shows the absolute Top-1 gain of fusion over CTC-only graphically (full numerical details are provided in Appendix B).


Figure 2: Analysis of fusion gain, hyperparameter sensitivity, and qualitative case studies. (a) Absolute Top-1 gain of fused score (α=0.4\alpha=0.4) over CTC-only scoring; C and L denote Conformer and LaBraM. (b) Candidate-set sensitivity for EEGAlign-LaBraM with varying negative sizes KK. (c) Sensitivity to the audio-alignment weight λaudio\lambda_{\mathrm{audio}} on RA. (d) Qualitative UMAP visualisation: EEGAlign (red dots) moves representations of CTC-only baseline (blue dots) toward ground-truth BGE-M3 embeddings (stars).


Two points are worth emphasising. (i) The fused score dominates the CTC-only score in every setting, confirming that the semantic embedding head and the CTC head provide complementary evidence at inference time. (ii) The magnitude of the gain depends strongly on paradigm and encoder: the largest gain (+11.54+11.54) is on PL with the LaBraM encoder, where CTC evidence is weak and the frozen BGE-M3 anchor is useful as a corrective signal (Table 4); the smallest gains (+1.5+1.5 to +4.4+4.4) are on RA and on the Conformer variants, where the CTC branch is already near-saturated. This is consistent with the view that text alignment functions mainly as a complementary inference-time score, rather than as a replacement for the CTC score.


Candidate-set sensitivity. Because the absolute Top-1 accuracy of closed-set identification depends mechanically on the candidate-pool size K+1K+1, we evaluate EEGAlign-LaBraM on both RA and PL under five candidate sizes (K∈{5,20,50,100,500}K\in\{5,20,50,100,500\}). As Figure 2(b) summarises, RA Top-1 degrades gracefully from 93.21%93.21\% at K=5K{=}5 to 67.50%67.50\% at K=500K{=}500, while PL Top-1 drops from 86.32%86.32\% to 16.38%16.38\%. Crucially, CRA@1 over chance grows with KK for both paradigms. Although direct comparisons warrant caution due to differences in language and stimuli, our PL results generally align with—and, under our closed-set sentence-identification protocol, outperform—representative auditory speech-perception decoding and ICASSP challenge-style match-mismatch systems [5, 27]. Full per-KK results are reported in Appendix C.2.


Audio-weight sensitivity. We also examine the model’s sensitivity to the audio-alignment weight λaudio\lambda_{\mathrm{audio}} on RA. As shown in Figure 2(c), the default gentler audio-alignment weight (λaudio=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{audio}}{=}0.1) yields slightly better Top-1 accuracy (82.37%82.37\% vs. 81.67%81.67\%) and lower Character Error Rate (17.26%17.26\% vs. 17.82%17.82\%) compared to the stronger setting λaudio=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{audio}}{=}0.5, indicating that while acoustic supervision is crucial, it should not overpower the primary CTC objective.


Representation-level structural alignment.
The fusion analysis above demonstrates that the semantic branch contributes useful inference-time evidence. We compute Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [18] between the upsampled EEG encoder output (d=256d{=}256, after the upsampler, before any projection head) and frozen BGE-M3 text embeddings (d=1024d{=}1024) on 200 held-out RA evaluation trials. The aggregate CKA results are reported in Appendix H; in brief, EEGAlign achieves the highest structural alignment, increasing linear CKA from 0.2940.294 to 0.3540.354 and RBF CKA from 0.3320.332 to 0.4020.402 relative to the CTC-only baseline, while each single-axis variant improves CKA only mildly. This supports the same conclusion as Table 2.


Figure 2(d) gives a compact qualitative view of this effect on representative rescued cases. The UMAP projection shows that EEGAlign moves the CTC-only baseline toward the correct BGE-M3 sentence anchor; the retained CKA summary and encoder-to-text representation measurements are provided in Appendices H and G.


Case-level retrieval comparison. Beyond the aggregate metrics, we inspect individual retrieval outcomes by examining the displayed case examples produced by EEGAlign, the CTC-only scoring baseline, and LaBraM-MSE (embedding-only retrieval without CTC). On 10 representative trials (5 RA, 5 PL) where both baselines fail at Top-1 but EEGAlign succeeds, the CTC-only baseline ranks the ground-truth sentence at positions 20–92 (median ∼\sim82) and LaBraM-MSE at positions 2–93, while EEGAlign places the correct sentence at rank 1 in every case. This indicates that text-audio alignment leverages complementary evidence: the alignment score and CTC log-likelihood provide strong sentence-level corrections to each other. Five cases for each paradigm and per-method rank comparisons are provided in Appendix I.1.

Appendix D Per-subject results


Tables 9–10 and Figure 3 report the per-subject Top-1 accuracy (closed-set, K=100K=100, seed = 42) at the best evaluation epoch for each training configuration, extracted directly from the training logs (the per-subject breakdown is emitted alongside every eval1/101 line as [eval][per_subject] sub-X top1=…n=…).


Three observations are worth highlighting. (i) The LaBraM + text-audio alignment model dominates all four RA subjects and all eight PL subjects uniformly: the subject-wise minimum on the best RA configuration (λaudio=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{audio}}{=}0.1) is 80.20%80.20\% (sub-m1), still +8+8 points above the best Conformer subject, and the PL minimum is 39.50%39.50\% (sub-06), also above every Conformer subject. (ii) The per-subject spread is small (RA std. 2.062.06 points, PL std. 1.671.67 points for the best LaBraM variant), indicating that the reported aggregate accuracy is not driven by one or two outlier subjects. (iii) The Conformer ablations reveal a paradigm-dependent effect of the auxiliary objectives: on RA, the full model is best for every subject while CTC-only remains stronger than either single-axis variant; on PL, the audio-only variant is the second-best aggregate configuration and improves over CTC-only for every listed subject, consistent with the weaker sequence-level signal in passive listening.

Appendix F Paradigm transfer analysis


Figure 4: Cross-paradigm transfer analysis. (a) 200-way in-batch Top-1 using the text head only, for every (training paradigm, evaluation paradigm) pair. Diagonal cells are the values reported in Figure 5; off-diagonal cells collapse to near chance. (b) Cosine margin Δ=cos+−cos−\Delta=\cos^{+}\!-\cos^{-} for the same four pairs, showing the same ordering of magnitude. Cross-paradigm alignment is essentially destroyed, supporting the paradigm-specific interpretation in Appendix G.

Appendix G Encoder-to-text representation analysis


How do the learned RA and PL encoder outputs align with text? Beyond the inference-time fusion gain, we directly compare the sentence-level EEG representations (e¯eeg\bar{e}_{\mathrm{eeg}}) from each paradigm to the frozen BGE-M3 ground-truth text embeddings. Evaluated on 200 held-out evaluation trials per paradigm (seed = 42) using the shared encoder bypass, we report two views: (i) cosine similarity between e¯eeg\bar{e}_{\mathrm{eeg}} and text embeddings for matched vs. mismatched pairs, and (ii) the 200-way text-only retrieval score (no CTC fusion). Table 12 reports both views, separately for the RA and PL checkpoints; Figure 5 summarises them graphically. All four panels of Figure 5 place the RA encoder (on RA data) and the PL encoder (on PL data) side by side, so the figure is a direct “RA encoder vs. PL encoder” comparison of the encoder output itself.

Figure 5: Encoder-feature text-alignment analysis for RA and PL paradigms. (a) Mean EEG–BGE-M3 cosine on matched vs. mismatched pairs. (b) Per-trial margin distribution. (c) 200-way retrieval curves using only the text head. (d) 200-way MRR and median rank. The cross-paradigm transfer matrix is in Appendix F.


Four observations follow from Table 12 and Figure 5. (i) Both paradigms yield encoders whose sentence-level representations are measurably aligned with BGE-M3: the cosine margin is +0.069+0.069 on RA and +0.051+0.051 on PL, and the 200-way text-only Top-1 is 48×48\times / 12×12\times above chance. So the text projection learns a non-trivial text-alignment on both RA and PL, not on RA alone. (ii) The alignment is nevertheless clearly stronger on RA: the margin is ∼35%\sim 35\% larger, the 200-way Top-1 is four times higher (24.0%24.0\% vs. 6.0%6.0\%), and the median rank on the full 4,000+ candidate gallery is roughly three times better (∼2%\sim\!2\% vs. ∼5.7%\sim\!5.7\% of the gallery). This is consistent with RA’s stronger sequence-level CTC signal: a well-decoded CTC branch makes the sentence-level pooled embedding a more reliable proxy for text semantics. (iii) The alignment is paradigm-specific: when we evaluate the RA encoder on PL data (or vice versa, Appendix F), the margin collapses by an order of magnitude (≤0.007\leq 0.007) and 200-way retrieval drops to 0.50.5–1.5%1.5\%, i.e. essentially chance. This justifies training separate RA and PL encoders rather than a single multi-paradigm model. (iv) The ordering “RA >> PL on alignment quality” matches the ordering “RA >> PL on closed-set Top-1” (Table 1) but not the ordering “PL >> RA on fusion gain” (Table 4). These two orderings are not contradictory: a weaker but still discriminative semantic channel can contribute more relative improvement on top of a noisier CTC branch than a stronger text score can on top of an already near-saturated CTC branch, which is exactly what we observe.


We keep the representation analysis compact and non-redundant: Table 12 gives the exact numerical measurements, Figure 5 provides the corresponding graphical summary, and Appendix F isolates the cross-paradigm transfer question. The larger diagnostic panels with additional t-SNE/PCA projections, embedding-norm histograms, and per-channel variance plots were used as sanity checks, but are omitted here because they repeat the same conclusion without changing the interpretation.

Appendix H CKA alignment of encoder outputs


Section 4.7 summarises the main CKA findings in text and uses the qualitative visualisation in Figure 2(d). This appendix provides the measurement protocol, exact numerical values, and one non-redundant four-condition CKA figure.


Protocol. We compute CKA between the upsampled EEG encoder output (enc_up, d=256d{=}256, after the ConvTranspose1D upsampler, before any projection head) and the frozen BGE-M3 sentence embeddings (d=1024d{=}1024) using 200 held-out RA evaluation trials (seed =42=42). We report both linear-kernel CKA and RBF-kernel CKA (σ\sigma set by the median heuristic). Because CKA is dimension-agnostic and the comparison is made before any alignment head is applied, the result reflects the internal encoder geometry and not an artefact of the projection training.


Results. Table 13 reports all four conditions.

Three observations follow. (i) Full EEGAlign achieves the highest CKA on both kernels, demonstrating that joint text-audio supervision shapes the encoder geometry and not just the final scoring rule. (ii) Each single-axis variant improves CKA modestly over the CTC-only baseline but does not jointly maximise CKA and Top-1 accuracy: notably, the text-CL-only condition reaches Linear CKA 0.3150.315 yet exhibits the lowest Top-1 (56.92%56.92\%), suggesting that text alignment alone may distort the CTC-useful acoustic geometry. (iii) The Full EEGAlign condition aligns both objectives: its CKA improvement (+0.060+0.060 linear, +0.070+0.070 RBF over CTC-only) is accompanied by the top closed-set Top-1. We interpret this as evidence that the two alignment heads act as mutual regularisers, each preventing the other from collapsing the encoder representation into a subspace that sacrifices the complementary signal.


Figure 6 shows the single CKA visualisation retained in the appendix, combining the linear/RBF measurements, their relation to Top-1 accuracy, and a compact bar summary in one panel.


Figure 6: CKA alignment analysis across all four ablation conditions. (a) Linear CKA between enc_up and BGE-M3 embeddings. (b) RBF CKA. (c) CKA vs. Top-1 scatter across conditions, showing that Full EEGAlign is the unique Pareto-optimal point. (d) Compact bar summary. All measurements use 200 held-out RA evaluation trials; the encoder output is taken before any projection head.
